DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Term.** By "biological father" I mean a human male who begot the child by natural generation. The KJV text gives Jesus a mother, a legal and supposed father, and a divine origin in the Holy Ghost. It never gives him a human begetter.

## 1. Matthew 1 breaks the "begat" pattern at the exact point of Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2-15 repeats *egennesen* (G1080, "begat"), male begetting male. In verse 16 the pattern changes. Joseph is called *aner* (G435, "husband"), not a begetter. The relative pronoun in "of whom" is *ex hes* (feminine singular, "out of whom"), so the birth is out of Mary alone.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". This is the unbroken pattern that verse 16 departs from.

**[L4]** The pattern runs "A begat B" fifteen generations running, then stops at Joseph. Joseph is Mary's husband, and the birth is "of whom," the woman. Matthew therefore does not say Joseph begat Jesus. It is the same Matthew who says in 1:18 and 1:20 why not.

## 2. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *gennethen* (G1080, "begotten/conceived") is the same verb family used for male begetting in verses 2-16. Here its source is *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Spirit." That is a source, and the phrase names no human male.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." Joseph knew he was not the father, so he considered divorce. The angel's correction in 1:20 gives the true source.

**[L4]** The same verb family is used for human begetting in 1:2-16 and for this conception in 1:20. Matthew assigns the source of the conception to the Holy Ghost, and Joseph's intent to put her away shows he was not the source. The text leaves no room for a human begetter.

## 3. "Before they came together" and "knew her not"

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *ginosko* (G1097, "to know"), used here of marital intimacy, is negated by *ouk* ("not") until the birth. This is also the key word in Mary's question.

**[L3]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The Greek is *andra ou ginosko*: *aner* (G435, "a male man") with *ginosko* negated. Mary says no male has known her.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception "before they came together," and 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" until after the birth. Mary herself says she has known no man. Together these two verses exclude a natural begetter before the birth.

## 4. The angel's answer in Luke names the mechanism

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *episkiazo* (G1982, "overshadow") is the verb of divine power. "Therefore" (*dio*, G1352, "for which reason") ties the title "Son of God" to the Holy Ghost's act and to no human generation.

**[L3]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." The woman is *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") when the angel comes.

**[L4]** Mary's question in 1:34 is about a human male, and the answer in 1:35 supplies a divine source in place of one. That answer explains the birth without a human father.

## 5. Scripture's promised seed is "her seed"

**[L1]** Genesis 3:15: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."

**[L2]** *zera* (H2233, "seed") is attributed to the woman. Scripture elsewhere traces seed through the man.

**[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law." The Greek is *genomenon ek gynaikos* (G1096 and G1135), "come to be out of a woman." The source named is a woman and no human male is joined to her.

**[L3]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." The body was prepared (*katartizo*, G2675, "fitted, made ready"), a divine act.

**[L4]** Genesis 3:15 gives the woman a seed, Galatians 4:4 says the Son was "made of a woman," and Hebrews 10:5 says the body was prepared by God. The pattern is consistent: Jesus' human nature comes from a woman by God's act, with no human male named.

## 6. Anticipated objections

**"Thy father" (Luke 2:48) and "the son of Joseph" (John 6:42).**

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**[L3]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Jesus immediately corrects whose father he means.

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543, "was supposed, was reckoned") marks a belief, an opinion held by people. It does not state a fact.

**[L1]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" The speakers are the Jews murmuring. Their phrase reports what they "know"; the text itself says "as was supposed."

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels the Joseph relation "supposed," and Luke 2:49 reassigns the title "Father." Joseph's role is legal and household headship, not begetting.

**"Seed of David / fruit of his loins" (Romans 1:3; Acts 2:30).**

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L1]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."

**[L2]** *ek spermatos* (G4690, "out of the seed") speaks of descent, and descent can run through the mother. Romans 1:3 uses *genomenon* (G1096, "made, come to be"), the same word as in Galatians 4:4 for "made of a woman."

**[L3]** Luke 3:31: "which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David." Luke's genealogy runs through Nathan, a different son of David from the line in Matthew 1:6-7, where Solomon's line runs to Joseph.

**[L4]** Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 use the same verb *genomenon*. Davidic descent "according to the flesh" is therefore carried by the woman, so a human male begetter is not required to supply it.

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Matthew's genealogy stops saying "begat" at Joseph and shifts to "of whom was born Jesus" (feminine *ex hes*, "out of whom"): [L1] Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus"; [L2] *egennesen* (begat) versus *ex hes* (out of her); [L3] Matthew 1:2 "Abraham begat Isaac".
2. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost," with Joseph excluded as source: [L1] Matthew 1:20 "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of the Holy Spirit); [L3] Matthew 1:19 Joseph "was minded to put her away privily."
3. Mary had known no man, and Joseph "knew her not" until the birth: [L1] Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son"; [L2] *ginosko* (to know) and *andra* (man, male); [L3] Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man."
4. The angel names the mechanism as the Holy Ghost's power: [L1] Luke 1:35 "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee"; [L2] *episkiazo* (overshadow) and *dio* (therefore); [L3] Luke 1:27 "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."
5. The "father" and "son of Joseph" language is supposed or legal, and the "seed of David" descent runs through the woman: [L1] Luke 3:23 "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph"; [L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed) and *genomenon* (made, come to be); [L3] Luke 2:49 "my Father's business" and Galatians 4:4 "made of a woman."
6. Christ had no biological human father: [L1] Matthew 1:18 "found with child of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of the Holy Spirit) as the stated source; [L3] Luke 1:35 "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# Round 2: Defender's answer

I answer each press by its own rows, then the question on Hebrews 7:14. I release some weight where the challenger is right.

## What I release (discipline)

- **[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman." **[L3]** Job 14:1: "Man [that is] born of a woman." **[L4]** Job 14:1 and Matthew 11:11 apply "of a woman" to men who had fathers, so Galatians 4:4 does not carry the exclusion alone. I withdraw it as load-bearing. It is consistent with my case and does not prove it.
- **[L3]** Genesis 3:15 "her seed" is supporting only, for the same reason (Genesis 4:25).
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19 carries intent and grounds, not a verb of knowing. My opening sentence "Joseph knew he was not the father" overstated. I restate it below as an inference from three rows.

## Against the challenge on D1: the verb stops at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."

**[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate, properly of the father, by extension of the mother") stands in the active, "begat," through verses 2-16 with a man as subject. At verse 16 it stands in the passive, "was born," with the child as subject and the woman as source (*ex hēs*, "out of whom").

**[L3]** Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." Matthew 1:6: "David the king begat Solomon of her [that had been the wife] of Urias."

**[L4]** The challenger is right that "of [a woman]" does not remove a father in 1:3, 1:5 and 1:6. In each of those verses a man is the subject of the active "begat" and the woman is added. In 1:16 Matthew keeps the active verb for Jacob and Joseph, then changes to the passive for Jesus, so no man is the subject of a begetting for him. The pattern that keeps the father when a woman is named in 1:3, 1:5 and 1:6 is the pattern 1:16 leaves.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise." This is Matthew's own signal that the manner of this birth differs from the preceding "begat" lines. The same passive verb of 1:16 returns in 1:20 with a named source.

## Against the challenge on D2: "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"

**[L2]** The sheet's gloss for *gennaō* is "properly, of the father," with "figuratively, to regenerate" listed separately. In 1:20 the object is "that which is begotten *in her*," in the womb. **[L1]** Matthew 1:18 puts the same fact as "found with child of the Holy Ghost"; **[L2]** *gastēr* (G1064, "womb") belongs to the physical state of being with child.

**[L3]** The challenger's 1 John 5:1 and John 1:13 are the figurative "regenerate" sense: believers "born... of God." **[L1]** John 1:13 says that birth is "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." **[L4]** John 1:13 sets "of God" against "of man" as the begetting source. It never places a figurative birth in a womb. In Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 the thing is "in her" and its source is "of the Holy Ghost," and no man is named as source. The challenger's reading of 1:20 as spiritual origin does not meet "found with child" (1:18).

**Joseph's knowledge (restated as inference).**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L2]** *paradeigmatizō* (G3856, "to expose to infamy") and *láthra* (G2977, "secretly") name a shame to be hidden. *dikaios* (G1342, "just, equitable") is why he would not take her as she was.
- **[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:23-24, the challenger's own rows: a betrothed damsel with a man is judged as "his neighbour's wife" humbled, and stoning follows.
- **[L4]** A husband who had known his wife and was the father would have no infamy to hide and no reason to put her away. The just man's plan answers a pregnancy he took to be from another. Matthew 1:20 then answers his fear ("fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife") by naming the source ("of the Holy Ghost"). A reason that removes the fear of a wrong must name a source other than a wrongdoer. This is the force of "for," and it works as a source notice by function.

## Against the challenge on D3: Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:18-25

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" **[L3]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb."

**[L4]** The challenger is right that the verb is present (*ginōskō*, G1097, "to know"). "This" in 1:34 is the conception of 1:31, and "how" asks its means. If the means were Joseph after the wedding, the question would have an obvious answer, and the angel gives a different one: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" (Luke 1:35). **[L1]** Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." That sentence has no work to do if a husband is to be the means. **[L3]** Luke 1:36 gives the sign, Elisabeth "who was called barren."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son." **[L2]** *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") is the word Matthew gives for the one who "shall be with child." **[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son," given as "a sign" in the same verse. **[L4]** A sign from the Lord that is an ordinary conception by a husband is no sign. The challenger has not answered Matthew 1:23.

**The order in Matthew 1:18-25.**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child." **[L1]** Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife." **[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- **[L2]** The negative with *ginōskō* in 1:25 is the verse's own statement of knowing and not knowing. "Came together" (*synerchomai*, G4905, "to come together") is the challenger's gloss for dwelling in one house, but 1:25 tells what "knew" means here.
- **[L4]** The challenger puts Joseph's knowing before the taking, within the espousal. He rests it on Deuteronomy 22:24 ("neighbour's wife"), which gives status and says nothing of intimacy. His other row is Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived," which is another couple. For Adam the text states the knowing. For Joseph and Mary it states "knew her not" (1:25), and the pregnancy stands before the angel and before the taking (1:18, 1:24). A knowing before the taking would be the cause of the "found with child" that 1:19 treats as shame and 1:20 as "of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:25 then protects the account: Joseph took her and still did not know her till the birth.

## Against the challenge on D4: Luke 1:35

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *eperchomai* (G1904, "to come upon") and *episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") are as the challenger says: presence and power. **[L3]** Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34, Acts 5:15.

**[L4]** I grant that those verbs, alone, are not begetting. They are not alone here. Three things fix their sense in Luke 1:35:

1. They answer the question "How shall this be?" (1:34), which is about a conception.
2. They are followed by *dio* (G1352, "therefore"), which ties the birth of "that holy thing... of thee" to the Holy Ghost's coming. The "therefore" falls inside the verse on the clauses it follows.
3. In Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34 the persons already exist. In Luke 1:35 the "therefore" attaches to a birth that has no other source named.

**[L3]** The challenger sends "therefore" back to 1:32 and the covenant title of 2 Samuel 7:14 and 1 Chronicles 28:6. **[L1]** Solomon is called "my son" with a named father in the same verse (1 Chronicles 28:6). **[L4]** In Luke 1:35 the angel gives the reason for the title as the Holy Ghost's act on Mary, and no man is named. The covenant parallel to Solomon explains the title. It does not explain why this answer to "how" names no man.

**[L3]** Psalm 2:7, Acts 13:33 and Romans 1:4 locate "begotten" at the raising. I do not rest on Psalm 2:7. Matthew 1:20 states a begetting in the womb, and Romans 1:4 says "declared [to be] the Son of God with power... by the resurrection," which declares a Sonship and does not locate the conception.

## Against the challenge on D5: seed, loins and Joseph's house

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L2]** *sperma* (G4690, "seed") in the sheet's gloss is "seed (including the male 'sperm'); by implication, offspring." **[L3]** Matthew 1:6: "David the king begat Solomon of her [that had been the wife] of Urias."

**[L4]** The word covers offspring across generations. David's "seed" and "loins" (Acts 2:30, *osphys*, G3751, "loins") reach a descendant about a thousand years on. **[L3]** Hebrews 7:5 uses "loins of Abraham" for all who "come out of" him, and those descendants had mothers of other houses. "Loins" names descent from David and does not require that the last link be a father.

**Mary's descent from David is not left to Luke 1:27.** I concede the KJV's clause "of the house of David" in Luke 1:27 can attach to Joseph, and I do not rest on it.

- **[L1]** Luke 1:32, said to Mary: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." **[L1]** Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." **[L1]** Luke 3:31: "which was [the son] of Nathan, which was [the son] of David." **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080) is the word of "born" in Matthew 1:16.
- **[L3]** Luke 3:23: "the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli." **[L3]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph."
- **[L4]** The KJV prints "[the son]" in brackets at Luke 3:23, supplied words. Matthew gives Joseph's begetter as Jacob, Luke names Heli. The challenger says Luke's line "runs to Nathan through Joseph's name," which sets two begetters over one man. If Joseph's line is Jacob's in Matthew, then Luke's second line, in which the child's descent from David comes through the child born "of thee," is Mary's side (Heli). The two lists name two houses by two ancestors, and "[the son]" in Luke 3:23 is added.

**The line through Solomon is cut for a male begetter.**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:11: "Josias begat Jechonias." **[L1]** Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel." **[L1]** Matthew 1:16 brings the line to Joseph.
- **[L3]** Jeremiah 22:24: "Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah." 1 Chronicles 3:16: "Jeconiah his son." Jeremiah 22:30: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
- **[L4]** Luke 1:32 promises this child the throne of David. A son begotten by Joseph, whose line passes through Jechonias (Matthew 1:11-12, 1:16), is "of his seed," and Jeremiah 22:30 says no man of that seed shall sit on David's throne. A child born "of thee" (Luke 1:35) and not begotten by Joseph is outside that seed, while Joseph's naming of him (Matthew 1:21, "thou shalt call his name JESUS"; 1:25) gives the legal side. This chain stands on two verses of Matthew, one of Chronicles and two of Jeremiah, and no row in the record answers it.

**"As was supposed" and "thy father."**

- **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** *nomizō* (G3543, "to deem, to think by custom") is rendered "supposed" by the KJV. **[L3]** Luke 2:44: "supposing him to have been in the company," and he was not. Acts 14:19: "supposing he had been dead," and he was not. **[L4]** In the same Gospel, a few verses before Luke 2:48, the KJV uses this word of a supposition that proved false. Acts 16:13 ("wont to be made") is a different sense of the same root, and the challenger offers no row to make Luke 3:23 that one. A narrator does not put "as was supposed" in parentheses at an ordinary father and son.
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." **[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" **[L3]** Luke 2:50: "And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them." **[L4]** Mary speaks of "thy father," and the reply gives the title to another Father. The two do not stand together as in 1 Chronicles 28:6, where the same speaker names both. Here the reply corrects the assumption.
- **[L1]** John 6:42: "whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" **[L3]** Luke 2:27 "the parents," Luke 2:33 "Joseph and his mother." **[L4]** Luke's own narration says "the parents" and "Joseph and his mother." The phrase "his father" is in the mouths of the people and of Mary speaking in worry.

## Against D6: the question on Hebrews 7:14

**[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."

**[L2]** *anatellō* (G393, "to arise, to spring up") says he arose out of Juda. It names the tribe and says nothing of which parent carries it.

**[L4]** How is it "evident"? By the public record. **[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Jacob begat Judas and his brethren." **[L1]** Luke 3:31 puts him in David's line by Nathan. **[L4]** Matthew 1:16 legally reckons him to Joseph, and Luke 1:32-35 and Luke 3:31 give the born-of-her line. Both are open to Judah.

**[L3]** Numbers 1:2 and 1:18 are a census of "every male by their polls," a muster list of men able to go to war. They are not a rule that a tribe passes only by a father. **[L3]** Numbers 27:8: "If a man die, and have no son, then ye shall cause his inheritance to pass unto his daughter." **[L3]** Numbers 36:8 keeps that daughter inside the "tribe of her father." **[L3]** Ezra 2:61 shows a man "called after their name," his wife's family. **[L4]** The law the challenger cites reckons through the father's house in the muster and lets house and name pass through a daughter in the cases it names. Ezra 2:62 is the penalty for not finding "their register," not a rule against the mother's line.
